reviewer.name: Claude Sonnet, fresh subagent (cold reader 2)
reviewer.origin: Claude Agent tool subagent, model sonnet, a fresh context with only this brief and its files, launched 2026-10-26 by session_01Mxpoi6tFT3FgKmBvtGjRtS (the writer's session)

evidence: Judged the draft “Think about what you want to do. Are there things you don’t want to do today?” against SOURCE.txt (replaced words “Get clear on what it is you want to do during the induction. What do you want not to do today?”; meaning to keep, from his published guide: “Choose the question or quality you want to explore, what you’re leaving alone today, and how much time you have.”) and in the paragraph that opens the “Before you begin” section. Change check: the_change says Emulate's first two sentences of the paragraph (sample cn) replace those two. DRAFT.txt is those two; they appear once in CONTEXT.txt as the paragraph's first two sentences, followed by the unchanged “How long do you want to spend on this?” and the bracket; the replaced words are gone; no AI-writer fix is claimed or visible. Meaning: the published guide's three items are still all asked, in order: what to work on (“what you want to do”, with the bracket's “You don't have to do this on a problem. You can do it on something you want to experience more of: love, play...” supplying the question-or-quality sense), what to leave alone today (“things you don’t want to do today”), and how much time (the unchanged third sentence). Differences from the replaced words, none of them a new claim: “Get clear on” becomes the lighter “Think about” (a small softening of the verb, but the decision is made later in the section by “Decide to do it.”); “during the induction” is dropped, so the first two sentences are less specific and “this” in the third sentence is the first explicit mention of the session, but the heading “Before you begin” and the bracket fix the reading at once, and the old words had the same “what it is you want to do” shape; the open “What do you want not to do today?” becomes the yes-no “Are there things you don’t want to do today?”, which allows a “no” but asks the same thing. No fact, step, condition or safety rule is added. Seam and voice: plain prompts in the same plain register as the neighbouring “How long do you want to spend on this?” and “Make sure you're leaving some time at the end to come back...”, and the bracket with its “whatever” keeps the human aside. I did not feel a different writer. It is more generic than the old “what it is you want to do / want not to do” phrasing, but it is not wrong or misleading. One mechanical mismatch, not a ground for the verdict: “don’t” in the draft is a curly apostrophe while “You don't” two sentences later in the same paragraph, and the rest of the section, use straight ones; it shows only in the raw text, but it should be made consistent where the sentences are put in. Tell rows: I went through T01 to T29 and C01 to C04 on the draft in context and find none actually happening in the draft's own words. Weighed hardest: T02 and T13 (the first three sentences are three short prompts in a row, each filling a slot of the published guide's three-item sentence, but this is a pre-session checklist, the swap keeps the same two jobs in the same two sentences, and the bracket is a real aside that is not slot-filling, so the swap neither adds a cadence nor removes a noticing); T12 and T26 (“want to do” and “don't want to do” are a mirrored pair and “want to” recurs in the next sentence, but the two halves are two different items of the published guide, a necessary contrast, and the old words repeated “want” the same way); T22 (a calm instructing voice, but it carries two real steps from his line, not reassurance, validation or anticipated feelings); T03 (the first item after the “read these pages” instruction under a “Before you begin” heading, so not abrupt); T06 and T23 (“things” is vague, but this is a checklist prompt, not therapy-abstract or scenery language); T10 (the “You don't have to...” formula is in the unchanged bracket, not in the draft); T15 (plain words, no rarer ones swapped in); T07, T19, T24 (no filler, announcement or self-answered question); T20, T28, T29 (the draft opens its paragraph; it is not a closer); C02 (“this” in the third sentence is the session, anchored by the heading and the bracket); C03 and C04 none. Linter B7 “short landing at paragraph end”: accepted. The linter saw the draft alone; in the paragraph, “Are there things you don’t want to do today?” is the second sentence, followed by “How long do you want to spend on this?” and the bracket, so it lands nothing. Linter D9 “follows the source order”: accepted; the two sentences are rewritten in place, so 1/1 agreement is by construction, and the T13 and T09 checks it asks for came out absent as above (the bracket is where the paragraph gives disproportionate attention). Linter E36/E41 “heavy second person”: accepted; 12.5 is two “you” in 16 words, one per sentence, and the replaced words also had two “you” (in 21 words), so the density comes from the draft being shorter, not from more address; the guide speaks to the reader as “you” throughout and these are the reader's own preparation questions. One note on the writer's ledger: its T03 line (“the sentence before it sets it up”) and its T14 and T15 lines (“puts back the author's own point that Emulate dropped”) are template wording that does not describe this draft, which opens its paragraph and is all Emulate's; it changes no judgment.
